All topics · Indian History · Lesson 6

Ashoka

Two sittings (read ~25 min one day, lesson ~25 min the next). One win: judge the claim "Ashoka's pacifism weakened India" from the book itself.

Why this lesson

Ashoka is the first Indian ruler we can hear in his own words. He had them cut into rocks and pillars across the subcontinent, and the Republic of India took one of his pillar capitals, the lions of Sarnath, as its state emblem. That makes him easy to admire and hard to judge: most of what we know about him, he chose to tell us. The question to carry through: when the main source is the king himself, how do you tell his policy from his publicity?

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Two of these were misses last time; the recap after them explains both.

Click where Pataliputra, Ashoka's capital, stood: on the south bank of the Ganga, in Bihar (within 200 km).

Pataliputra is modern Patna, on the Ganga in Bihar, in the old heartland of Magadha.

Ashoka's thirteenth rock edict says 100,000 people were killed in the Kalinga war. Which of these, if it existed, would corroborate that number?

A copy of the edict, or another edict by the same king, is the same witness speaking twice. A Buddhist chronicle has its own reason to make the conversion dramatic. Only an independent source counts, which is why Megasthenes' tower spacing matching the Arthashastra's rule mattered in lesson 5.

Recap: corroboration, and where the Maurya heartland was
  • Corroboration means two sources with different authors and different purposes agree. In lesson 5, Megasthenes said Pataliputra's wall had 570 towers and 64 gates. That's believable not because excavators have traced the whole wall (they've only found stretches of its timber palisade) but because the German scholar Dieter Schlingloff showed the tower spacing matches the 54 yards the Arthashastra prescribes. A Greek ambassador and an Indian manual on statecraft had no reason to copy each other.
  • Pataliputra is modern Patna, on the Ganga in Bihar. Magadha, the kingdom it ruled, was the eastern Ganges plain.
  • Whose voice? Last lesson's warm-up asked who speaks in the Rigveda (the priests). Ask the same of every source in this lesson: who wrote it, for whom, and why.

Block 1: read first

Reading

Kulke & Rothermund, A History of India, Chapter Two, "Ashoka, the Beloved of the Gods" (the whole section, about 7 pages), including its two boxed quotations, "Ashoka's supremacy: surveillance" and "'All men are my children' – Ashoka's welfare policy", and Map 2.1.

Then read the first two paragraphs of the next section, "The end of the Maurya empire and the northern invaders": from its start to "…the Vedic horse sacrifice" (about one page). The lesson's claim needs them.

Name traps: Ashoka calls himself Devanampiya Piyadasi, "Beloved of the Gods, of gracious mien"; he rarely uses the name Ashoka. Dhamma is the Prakrit form of Sanskrit dharma; K&R translate it "right conduct". Mahamatra means a high officer; a Dhamma-Mahamatra is one assigned to right conduct.

Answer the boxes below as you read, a sentence or two each. They're your notes; every answer gets a reply.

What did the conquest of Kalinga cost, by Ashoka's own count, and what did he do afterwards that he had not done before? Name one thing he did not do.

Cost: 150,000 abducted, 100,000 killed, many more died later. Afterwards: gave up further wars of conquest, became a Buddhist lay follower, went on a 256-day pilgrimage, spread right conduct through edicts and envoys. Did not: give Kalinga back or return the abducted people; did not publish his remorse (Rock Edict XIII) in Kalinga itself. Reading note, not graded for mastery.

Who were the Pativedakas and the Dhamma-Mahamatras, and why did Ashoka say they could reach him at any hour?

Pativedakas: reporters who checked government institutions and reported to Ashoka. Dhamma-Mahamatras: taught right conduct and supervised the people in it, including inside his relatives' households. Any hour: he wanted constant information and quick decisions (the surveillance box); his orders were being resisted ("virtuous deeds are difficult to accomplish"). Either reason.

K&R say the usual map of Ashoka's empire is too big. What evidence do they use, and what does it show?

The findspots of his inscriptions: clusters in the centre and on the frontiers, none in the vast interior. So much of present Maharashtra, Andhra, Kerala and Tamil Nadu was not administered; south of the Vindhyas the Mauryas held coasts and an enclave near the gold region; forest tribes in the interior were unconquered. Any two points.

What surprised or confused you in the reading? (Optional.)

No right answer. Reply to it.

Block 2: the lesson

1. Reading an edict: who speaks, for whom, why (from the reading)

An edict is not a diary. It's a public text the king paid stonecutters to carve where officials would read it aloud. K&R give us one test case that shows how carefully Ashoka chose what to say to whom. Try to answer each step's question before opening the next.

Who speaks? The king, in the first person: "Thus speaks King Devanampiya Piyadasi". Nobody else's view of Kalinga survives. The victims, the soldiers and the Kalinga court are silent.

For whom? Rock Edict XIII, with its remorse for Kalinga, was cut on rocks in the frontier provinces, from Kandahar to the south. Its readers were his officials and subjects there, and the neighbours he names (Greek kings, the Cholas and Pandyas).

What changes in Kalinga itself? At Dhauli and Jaugada, the two edict sites in Kalinga, Rock Edict XIII is left out. In its place are the "separate edicts": "All men are my children", and orders to officials to treat the borderers well. K&R: "as an astute politician, he also did not express his contrition" there.

So why? (judgment, K&R's and mine) To distant readers, remorse shows a king who conquers by right conduct. To the conquered, it would admit the war was a crime while he kept the land and the 150,000 captives. Same king, same year, two messages, each fitted to its audience. That's the habit to build: read an edict as a message aimed at someone.

Why does the Kalinga copy of the rock edicts leave out Ashoka's famous remorse for the Kalinga war, according to K&R?

K&R call it the act of "an astute politician": he never thought of giving up Kalinga or returning the abducted people, and he addressed Kalinga with the "separate edicts" instead.

Rock Edict XIII is our main source on the Kalinga war. Which of these can it show on its own, and which need another source?

An edict is perfect evidence of its own message: what the king said and wanted believed. Everything that happened outside the text, including the casualty count, the victims' view and whether orders were obeyed, needs a witness who isn't the king.

2. Dhamma as policy, not only belief (from the reading)

Ashoka's conversion is a famous story. K&R's point is that what followed was also a program of government. Here is the sequence, in K&R's dates (they follow the Dutch scholar Eggermont, who dates the reign 268–233 BC; other books shift these by a year or two):

| Year (BC) | What happened | |---|---| | 261 | Conquest of Kalinga | | 259 | 256-day pilgrimage to the Buddhist holy places | | 258 | Missionary program begins; minor rock edicts ordered | | 257 | First four of the fourteen major rock edicts | | 13th year of the reign | Pativedakas and Dhamma-Mahamatras appointed; envoys sent to the Greek kings |

Was dhamma just Buddhism? No. Ashoka confessed his Buddhist faith in the minor edicts, but he "carefully avoided equating his doctrine of right conduct with Buddhism as such" and supported Brahmins and the Ajivikas too. Dhamma was a code of conduct for all subjects: no needless killing of animals, respect for elders and teachers, no immoral gatherings.

How was it enforced? By officers. Governors and district officers had to tour regularly to check that right conduct was followed. When that met resistance ("virtuous deeds are difficult to accomplish"), he created two new kinds of officers, who reported straight to him at any hour.

Where were they posted? Everywhere, "in the private rooms of my brothers and sisters and all of my relatives". Relatives were exactly where a challenge to the throne would come from. K&R's verdict: these officers "were different in name only from Kautalya's spies". The Arthashastra's methods, under a new name.

Why would an emperor want this? K&R, following the Indian historian Romila Thapar: an empire this size could not rest on "the naked power politics of the Arthashastra"; it needed a deeper legitimation. Dhamma gave every subject, of every sect, a reason to accept one king, and gave the king a reason to watch every subject.

Which piece of evidence from the reading best shows that Ashoka's dhamma was a policy of government, not only his private faith?

Lay membership, the pilgrimage and the remorse all show belief. A corps of officers with access to the king, posted in his relatives' households, is a state apparatus.

K&R say the Dhamma-Mahamatras "were different in name only from Kautalya's spies". What is the strongest reason they give?

Posting them "in the private rooms of my brothers and sisters and all of my relatives" put watchers exactly where a rival claimant would plot. The other three options aren't in the reading: Ashoka names these officers openly in his edicts.

Put these in order, earliest first (K&R's dates).

3. How big was the empire, really? (from the reading)

Most maps colour almost the whole subcontinent Maurya. K&R test that against the one kind of evidence Ashoka left everywhere he ruled: his inscriptions.

Notice where they are: on the frontiers, and none at the centre. Pillar edicts cluster in the Ganges heartland instead; minor rock edicts cluster in the south. In between lies a huge interior with no Ashokan inscription at all.

The five parts. A core (Magadha and the old mahajanapadas) ruled directly, and four provinces under princes as viceroys: the northwest from Taxila, the west from Ujjain, the east from Tosali in Kalinga, the south from Suvarnagiri ("gold mountain").

The gaps. No inscriptions across most of present Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh, or in Kerala and Tamil Nadu. South of the Vindhyas the Mauryas held the coasts, the trade routes and an enclave near the gold.

The unconquered. Forest peoples (atavi) lived in the interior. Ashoka announced his power to them and demanded their submission "that they may not be killed". The man who renounced conquest still threatened force at home.

How many provinces governed by princes (viceroys) does K&R's reading of the inscriptions give, besides the central region the emperor ruled himself? (A fifth is sometimes proposed, from one inscription; K&R doubt it.)

Four: Taxila (northwest), Ujjain (west), Tosali (east, in Kalinga), Suvarnagiri (south). The Panguraria inscription addresses a prince only about 110 miles from Ujjain, so he may simply be Ujjain's viceroy.

Why do K&R conclude that much of the interior of the subcontinent was not administered by the Mauryas?

It's an argument from distribution: inscriptions mark where his officials worked. Absence isn't proof, and K&R say so, but after a century of searching the pattern is unlikely to change. The edicts do mention "unconquered" areas and forest tribes, but not as a list of regions.

4. The claim: "Ashoka's pacifism weakened India" (from the reading, then beyond it)

You'll meet this in arguments about Indian nationalism and the military: Ashoka gave up war, the army went soft, and invaders walked in. The empire did end about 50 years after his death: in 185 BC the general Pushyamitra Shunga killed the last Maurya king during a parade of the troops.

Put these in order, earliest first.

Bimbisara (5th century BC) → Chandragupta (c. 320 BC) → Kalinga (261 BC) → Pushyamitra (185 BC). The first item is from lesson 5's text; the other three are from this lesson's reading and the paragraph above.

Beyond the reading, three classic positions (summarised from secondary accounts; I haven't read the originals, so treat the labels as a starting point):

  • Haraprasad Shastri (early 20th century): Ashoka's pro-Buddhist policy, like the ban on animal sacrifice, provoked a Brahmin reaction; Pushyamitra, a Brahmin, was its result.
  • H. C. Raychaudhuri, Political History of Ancient India (1923): rejected the Brahmin-reaction story (the Mauryas had a Brahmin commander-in-chief) and criticised Ashoka as an impractical idealist whose policy weakened the state's military edge.
  • Romila Thapar, Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961): the causes were structural, a highly centralised administration that only worked under strong kings, and weak successors.

Using the reading, give (1) one fact showing Ashoka was not a pacifist in practice, (2) one fact about what happened after his death that bears on the claim, and (3) K&R's own judgment of his decision to stop conquering, in your words. Then give your verdict on the claim, in a sentence.

Grades exactly the three named parts, from the reading only. (1) Not a pacifist in practice: kept Kalinga and never returned the 150,000 abducted; threatened forest tribes with death unless they submitted; kept his army and administration (K&R credit his success partly to "the strength of his army and administration"); placed watchers in relatives' households. Any one. (2) After his death: the distant provinces probably became independent (no sign of Maurya rule in the south or Kalinga after him); the centre may have been divided among sons and grandsons; no successor issued major edicts (perhaps resentment of their paternal tone); Buddhist texts claim decay began in his last years but K&R say that view "is not generally accepted"; the last Maurya was killed in 185 BC, about 50 years later. Any one, with what it suggests (e.g. collapse came under weaker successors, not right after him). (3) K&R: his "greatness was due to his insight into the futility of further expansionist warfare", which would have cost many bloody wars and blocked consolidation (Aurangzeb, who tried, broke the Mughal empire). Paraphrase is fine. Verdict: any reasoned verdict. Got it = all three parts, no false statement. Naming Shastri, Raychaudhuri or Thapar earns credit, never required.

Extra practice (optional)

  • Reading: the two boxed edicts once more. For each, answer: who is addressed, what does the king want them to do or believe, and what would an independent source need to show to confirm it? (K&R Ch. 2.)
  • Extra reading: Rock Edict XIII and the two Kalinga separate edicts, whole, in S. Dhammika's free translation, The Edicts of King Asoka (Buddhist Publication Society, 1993), about 5 pages. Compare the tone of the two Kalinga texts with XIII. Read it on Access to Insight. The translator warns that many passages are unclear and translations disagree.
  • Extra article: the reading itself points to it: Romila Thapar's Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (Oxford, 1961; later editions). Its last chapter is on the decline. Not in your library; tell me if you'd like it added to the books-needed list.
